paragraphs.heading: What a divisor is
paragraphs.text: A divisor of an integer n, which people also call a factor of n, is an integer m that you can multiply by some integer to get n. In that case n is a multiple of m, and n is divisible by m, which means dividing n by m leaves no remainder. For example, 7 × 6 = 42, so 7 is a divisor of 42, written 7 ∣ 42. You can also say 7 divides 42, or 42 is a multiple of 7.

paragraphs.heading: Positive, negative and trivial
paragraphs.text: Divisors can be negative as well as positive, though people often mean only the positive ones. The number 4 has six divisors, 1, 2, 4, −1, −2 and −4, but usually only 1, 2 and 4 are mentioned. Every integer n is divided by 1, −1, n and −n, which are called its trivial divisors; any other divisor is non-trivial. Any nonzero integer that has a non-trivial divisor is a composite number. A prime number, by contrast, is a positive integer with exactly two positive factors: 1 and itself.

paragraphs.heading: Rules divisors follow
paragraphs.text: Divisibility passes along a chain: if a divides b and b divides c, then a divides c. If a divides both b and c, it also divides their sum b + c and their difference b − c. But two divisors of a number need not add up to another divisor: 2 and 3 both divide 6, yet 5 does not. Euclid's lemma says that if a divides bc and gcd (a, b) = 1, then a divides c.

paragraphs.heading: Proper divisors
paragraphs.text: A positive divisor of n that is not n itself is called a proper divisor, or an aliquot part. The proper divisors of 6, for instance, are 1, 2 and 3. Adding up the proper divisors sorts numbers into three kinds. If the sum equals n, the number is perfect; if the sum is smaller, it is deficient; and if the sum is bigger, it is abundant.

paragraphs.heading: Counting divisors
paragraphs.text: The number of positive divisors of n is written d (n). When m and n are relatively prime, d (m n) = d (m) × d (n). For instance, 42 has eight divisors, 1, 2, 3, 6, 7, 14, 21 and 42, and 8 = d (2) × d (3) × d (7). This can break down when m and n share a common divisor. On average, a randomly chosen positive integer n has about ln n divisors, though that figure comes from the share contributed by numbers with unusually many divisors.
